absolute error: The absolute value of the difference between an approximate value and the true value.
annuity: A financial product involving equal regular payments, whose total is found using a geometric series.
approximation: A value close to but not exactly equal to the true value of a measurement or calculation.
arithmetic sequence: A sequence in which the difference between consecutive terms is constant.
arithmetic series: The sum of the terms of an arithmetic sequence.
common difference, d: The constant difference between consecutive terms of an arithmetic sequence.
common logarithm: The logarithm to base 10, usually written log(x).
common ratio, r: The constant ratio between consecutive terms of a geometric sequence.
compound interest: Interest calculated on both the principal and accumulated interest, producing a geometric sequence of balances.
compounding frequency, k: The number of times per year that interest is added to the principal.
exponent / index: The number indicating how many times a base is multiplied by itself.
exponential growth model: A model of the form P(t) = P0 e^(kt) or P0 r^t, describing growth or decay over time.
fractional exponent: An exponent that is a fraction, representing a root combined with a power.
future value, fv: The value a present sum will grow to after earning interest over time.
geometric sequence: A sequence in which the ratio between consecutive terms is constant.
half-life: The time for a decaying quantity to fall to half its initial value.
laws of exponents: The rules for multiplying, dividing, and raising powers, such as a^m times a^n equals a^(m+n).
laws of logarithms: The rules for the logarithm of a product, quotient, and power.
logarithm: The inverse of exponentiation, where log_a(b) = c means a^c = b.
logarithmic transformation: Taking logarithms of data to turn an exponential relationship into a linear one.
natural logarithm: The logarithm to base e, written ln(x), where e is approximately 2.718.
percentage error: The relative error expressed as a percentage of the true value.
present value, pv: The current worth of a future sum, found by discounting it back to today.
relative error: The absolute error divided by the true value, giving a unitless measure of accuracy.
rounding: Replacing a number with the nearest value at a specified place, rounding up at 5 or above.
The meaningful digits of a number, starting from the first non-zero digit, that convey precision.
simple interest: Interest calculated only on the original principal, producing an arithmetic sequence of balances.
standard form / scientific notation: Writing a number as a value between 1 and 10 times a power of ten.
truncation: Cutting off digits after a certain place without rounding.
asymptote: A straight line that a curve approaches ever more closely but never reaches.
carrying capacity, l: The maximum value a logistic model approaches as time grows large.
coefficient of determination, r²: A value between 0 and 1 indicating how well a regression model explains the data's variation.
composite function: A function f(g(x)) in which one function's output is the input of another.
continuity: The property of a graph having no breaks or jumps.
discriminant, δ: The quantity b^2 - 4ac determining the number of real roots of a quadratic.
domain: The set of input values for which a function is defined.
doubling time: The time for an exponentially growing quantity to double, equal to ln(2)/k.
exponential decay model: A model of the form f(t) = A e^(kt) with k negative, in which the value approaches zero over time.
function: A relation assigning each input exactly one output.
gradient / slope: A value measuring a line's steepness and direction, the change in y over the change in x.
horizontal line test: A test for whether a function is one-to-one, met if no horizontal line crosses the graph more than once.
inflection point: The point on a logistic curve where growth is fastest, occurring at half the carrying capacity.
inverse function: A function reversing another, so that f(a) = b gives the inverse mapping b back to a.
linear function: A function of the form f(x) = mx + c whose graph is a straight line.
logistic function: An S-shaped function that grows exponentially at first and then levels off at a carrying capacity.
one-to-one function: A function in which different inputs always give different outputs.
piecewise function: A function defined by different rules over different intervals of its domain.
quadratic function: A function of the form f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c whose graph is a parabola.
range: The set of output values a function actually produces.
regression: A statistical method finding the function that best fits a set of data points.
vertical line test: A test for whether a graph is a function, met if no vertical line crosses it more than once.
ambiguous case: The situation where two sides and a non-included angle may yield zero, one, or two triangles.
angle in 3d space: An angle between lines or between a line and a plane in a three-dimensional figure.
angle of depression: The angle measured downward from the horizontal to an object below.
angle of elevation: The angle measured upward from the horizontal to an object above.
area formula: The formula giving a triangle's area as half the product of two sides and the sine of their included angle.
bearing: A direction measured clockwise from north, written as a three-digit angle.
composite solid: A figure made by combining or removing basic solids.
cosine rule: The relation c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab cos C used to solve triangles given two sides and the included angle or all three sides.
dihedral angle: The angle between two planes measured perpendicular to their line of intersection.
heron's formula: A formula giving a triangle's area from its three side lengths using the semi-perimeter.
included angle: The angle lying between two given sides of a triangle.
inverse trigonometric function: A function that returns an angle from a known trigonometric ratio.
perpendicular bisector: The line passing through a segment's midpoint at right angles to it, equidistant from its endpoints.
sine rule: The relation a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C used to solve triangles with matching side-angle pairs.
slant height, l: The distance along the sloping surface of a cone or pyramid from apex to base edge.
space diagonal: The diagonal of a rectangular solid joining opposite corners through its interior.
step-by-step decomposition: A strategy for solving 3D problems by breaking them into identified cross-sections and stages.
surface area: The total area of all faces of a three-dimensional solid.
surveying: The practical use of trigonometry to measure distances, angles, and positions of features.
trigonometric ratios: The sine, cosine, and tangent defined as ratios of sides in a right triangle.
volume: The amount of space a three-dimensional solid occupies, measured in cubic units.
voronoi cell: The region of points closest to a particular site, forming a convex polygon.
voronoi diagram: A division of the plane into regions each containing the points closest to a given site.
voronoi vertex: A point where three or more Voronoi cells meet, equidistant from three sites.
box plot / box-and-whisker diagram: A diagram displaying the five-number summary of a data set with a box and whiskers.
chi-squared test of independence: A test of whether two categorical variables are independent, comparing observed and expected frequencies.
conditions for using normal distribution: The conditions under which a binomial distribution may be approximated by a normal distribution.
convenience sampling: Selecting easily accessible individuals, which is quick but prone to strong bias.
expected frequency, e: The frequency expected in each cell of a contingency table if the variables were independent.
explanatory & response variable: The explanatory variable predicts, while the response variable is the one being predicted.
extrapolation: Using a regression line to predict beyond the range of the data, which is unreliable.
h₀ and h₁: The null hypothesis of independence and the alternative hypothesis of dependence in a chi-squared test.
interpolation: Using a regression line to predict within the range of the data, which is relatively reliable.
least-squares regression line: The line minimizing the sum of squared vertical distances from the data points.
lurking variable: A hidden third variable affecting both variables, creating correlation without causation.
measures of central tendency: Summary values representing the center of a data set, such as the mean, median, and mode.
measures of dispersion: Values describing how spread out data are, such as range, interquartile range, and standard deviation.
outlier: A data value lying more than 1.5 times the interquartile range below Q1 or above Q3.
pearson's correlation coefficient, r: A value from -1 to 1 measuring the strength and direction of a linear relationship.
scatter diagram: A graph plotting paired values of two variables to reveal their relationship.
significance level & p-value: The threshold for rejecting the null hypothesis and the probability of a result at least as extreme.
simple random sampling: Selecting individuals so that every member of the population has an equal chance of being chosen.
standardisation & z-score: Converting a value to a standard normal score showing how many standard deviations it lies from the mean.
stratified sampling: Dividing a population into strata and sampling from each in proportion to its size.
systematic sampling: Selecting every kth item from a list as a sample.
antiderivative & indefinite integral: An antiderivative F has derivative f; the indefinite integral is the general antiderivative plus a constant.
average rate of change: The average rate of change of a function between two points, equal to the slope of the secant line.
constraint: An equation relating variables in a real-world context, used to reduce the objective function to one variable.
definite integral & area: A definite integral gives the signed area between a curve and the x-axis over an interval.
first derivative test: Classifying a stationary point by the sign change of the first derivative around it.
fundamental theorem of calculus: The theorem that a definite integral equals the antiderivative evaluated at the upper limit minus the lower.
initial condition: A known point used to determine the constant of integration in an antiderivative.
instantaneous rate of change & derivativ: The rate of change at a single point, equal to the slope of the tangent line.
integration notation: The symbols used in integration, including the integral sign, integrand, and limits.
integration of polynomials: Integrating each term of a polynomial by raising the exponent by one and dividing by the new exponent.
intervals of increase & decrease: Intervals where a function rises (f' positive) or falls (f' negative).
negative & fractional exponents: Rewriting negative and fractional exponents before applying the power rule.
numerical differentiation with gdc: Using a calculator's numerical derivative function to evaluate a derivative at a point.
objective function: The quantity to be maximized or minimized, expressed in terms of one variable.
over- & underestimate: Whether the trapezoidal rule over- or underestimates the true area, determined by the curve's concavity.
power rule: The rule that the derivative of ax^n is anx^(n-1).
second derivative test: Classifying a stationary point by the sign of the second derivative there.
stationary point: A point where the derivative is zero, which may be a maximum, minimum, or inflection point.
tangent & normal: The tangent is a line touching a curve with its slope; the normal is perpendicular to the tangent.
trapezoidal rule: A numerical method estimating the area under a curve by dividing it into trapezoids.
